confirmed.summary: scene_retake_rows / scene_shot_windows include every beat matching the scene number, even ones with no rendered clip, and give their (purely nominal) shots real-looking Scene-In/Out timecodes that collide with whatever beat actually occupies that time in the stitched video.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Normal mid-production state: 1.B1 is rendered+approved, 1.B2 hasn't fired yet (or failed), 1.B3 then renders and the scene gets re-stitched (cb_beats.run's 'GATE-3 REVIEW COPY' block fires this automatically after every render). beat_address_map computes 1.B2's shot list purely from its authored cuts[] via _v5_shot_time_ranges — regardless of whether it has a clip — so it gets non-empty start_sec/end_sec. Because 1.B2's 'duration' is 0 (no clip on disk), the cumulative offset carried into 1.B3 is unaffected, but 1.B2's ghost shot rows are still emitted at that same offset, i.e. the exact window 1.B3's real shots now occupy. In the CSV, two different beats' rows claim identical Scene In/Out times. Worse, cb_post.burn_review_overlay's _active_label(windows, t) returns the FIRST window in list order whose scene_in<=t<scene_out; since 1.B2 (never rendered) precedes 1.B3 in beat order, its ghost window wins the collision and gets burned into the review video's on-screen label while 1.B3's real footage is actually playing — a reviewer marking up the retake sheet would be pointed at the wrong beat/shot.
confirmed.proposedFix: In scene_address_map (or scene_retake_rows/scene_shot_windows directly), skip a beat's shots entirely when beat_address_map's own 'rendered' flag is False — an unrendered beat contributes zero real footage to the stitched review video, so its shot list is a plan, not elapsed time, and should never compete for a Scene-In/Out slot with an actually-rendered later beat.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified directly against the current code (engine/cb_address.py) and reproduced the exact collision live.

beat_address_map (lines 86-109) computes a beat's `shots[]` purely from its authored `cuts[]` via `cb_segprompt._v5_shot_time_ranges` whenever the beat ships the v5 "raw" prompt — this path runs unconditionally, with no check on the `rendered` flag (line 72, computed separately from `os.path.exists(clip)`). So an unrendered/failed beat still gets real-looking `start_sec`/`end_sec` on every shot, while its `duration` is 0.0 (from `_clip_duration` returning 0.0 for a missing file).

scene_retake_rows (139-159) and scene_shot_windows (161-173) then walk every beat matching the scene number (via scene_address_map, which does not filter on `rendered`), only skipping a *shot* if `start_sec` is literally absent — never skipping a whole beat for being unrendered — and advance a running `offset` by `bm.get("duration") or 0.0`. An unrendered beat contributes 0.0 to the offset (never advancing it) while still emitting shot windows *at* that un-advanced offset, so the next actually-rendered beat's real windows start at the identical offset — a guaranteed collision whenever a beat is skipped/fails between two rendered beats.

I reproduced this directly: built a 3-beat scratch package (1.B1 rendered 13s, 1.B2 never rendered, 1.B3 rendered 15s) and called cb_address.scene_shot_windows for real. Output confirmed exactly the claimed collision — 1.B2's ghost windows (13.0-21.0, 21.0-28.0) exactly overlap 1.B3's real windows (13.0-21.0, 21.0-28.0). Feeding this into cb_post._active_label(windows, t) (the actual function burn_review_overlay uses, cb_post.py:192-196, which returns the FIRST list match) confirmed it returns "BEAT 2 SHOT 1/2" for t=16..27 — the exact window where 1.B3's real footage is actually playing in the stitched video, since 1.B2 appears earlier in beat order and thus earlier in the windows list.

I also traced how this becomes reachable in production: cb_beats.run's full-scene path (codes=None, e.g. a whole-scene rebuild) stitches whatever made it into `clips` with no completeness check — if a middle beat fails via any of its several `continue` points (Law-5 voice refusal, manifest BLOCK, missing anchor, render failure) while flanking beats succeed, `clips` silently contains only the successful beats and `stitch()` is called directly, producing a real stitched video that skips the failed beat. The unconditional "GATE-3 REVIEW COPY" tail (cb_beats.py:546-556) then rebuilds the review overlay from a freshly computed scene_shot_windows() that includes the failed beat's ghost shots regardless. Even in the codes=[code] subset-regen path (the normal walk_scene/fire_next_beat production flow), a previously-rejected-and-archived beat (rule 44's rejection mechanism removes its clip from disk) reproduces the same scenario against a stale-but-existing `_stitched` file, since the review-copy block only checks `os.path.exists(_stitched)`, not whether the current beat set is complete.

This is a real, concrete, reachable correctness bug, not a false alarm — the proposed fix (skip a beat's shots when its own `rendered` flag is False) directly and correctly addresses the root cause.

confirmed.summary: The total_frames clamp added 2026-07-09 to protect cb_retake.splice_shot() from an out-of-range frame_end was only applied to the v5/raw shot-timing branch; the legacy action_timeline branch a few lines below computes frame_start/frame_end the same nominal way with no clamp at all.

Its last shot's frame_end = int(round(tr[1]*fps)) can then point past the real clip's last frame, and cb_retake.regen_shot/splice_shot (the documented consumer of frame_start/frame_end) would target a range beyond end-of-file for that shot's retake splice.
confirmed.proposedFix: Apply the same 'if total_frames: clamp frame_start/frame_end to total_frames' logic (currently only at lines 106-108) to the legacy branch's frame_start/frame_end assignment (lines 119-120) too, or move the clamp to run once after either branch has populated a shot dict.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Read the exact code at engine/cb_address.py:86-123 (current working-tree state, matching `git diff HEAD` which shows this is the uncommitted 2026-07-09 change). Confirmed the finding precisely:

- Lines 87-109 (the `if g.get("raw"):` branch, v5/DEFINITIVE_PROSE path): computes `frame_start`/`frame_end` from `cb_segprompt._v5_shot_time_ranges`'s nominal per-cut split, then explicitly clamps both to `total_frames` when the clip has been measured (lines 106-108), with a comment stating the exact rationale: "a generative render is never guaranteed to pace exactly to that nominal split... a real risk for cb_retake.splice_shot()."
- Lines 111-121 (the `else` branch, legacy `action_timeline` path): computes `frame_start`/`frame_end` from `parse_time_range(st.get("time"))` — the exact same class of nominal (not measured) timing data — with NO clamp applied at all.

This is a genuine asymmetry, not an intentional design split: both branches populate the identical `shots[]` shape consumed by the same downstream function, `cb_retake.regen_shot`/`splice_shot` (verified directly — `regen_shot` reads `sh["frame_start"]`/`sh["frame_end"]` with no bounds-checking of its own, and `splice_shot`'s ffmpeg filter graph uses `fe` to trim the beat's tail segment and to compute the replacement's slot length). The stated rationale for the clamp (a generative render's real duration can undershoot its nominal request) applies identically to both prompt builders — nothing about the legacy compact/JSON builder makes its declared `action_timeline` times any more reliably matched to actual rendered frame count.

I confirmed the legacy branch is a real, intentionally-kept fallback (not dead code): `cb_seedance.get_seedance_prompt` explicitly falls back to the "cb_seedance compact" builder (`raw` unset) whenever `cb_segprompt.shipped_prompt` raises (including the documented `ManifestFieldMissing` case, caught explicitly at cb_seedance.py's own except block), or when the beat/scene lookup fails — a real, reachable path per the function's own docstring, not something already retired by the v1-v4 purge (rule 40/42, which removed a different builder entirely).

This is precisely the class of gap this codebase's own standing rule 11 ("sweep the same pattern across every module, not just the one file where it was noticed") exists to catch, and the proposed fix (apply the same clamp logic to the legacy branch, or hoist it to run once after either branch populates a shot) is correct, minimal, and consistent with the existing pattern. I do not find a basis to refute this as a false alarm.

confirmed.summary: scene_retake_rows and scene_shot_windows are two near-identical copy-pasted loops — same beat/shot walk, same cumulative-offset accumulation, same 'start_sec not in sh' guard — differing only in the shape of the dict each appends.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Any future fix to the shared iteration/offset logic (e.g. the unrendered-beat filter in the first finding above) has to be applied twice in near-identical code; it's easy for one copy to get updated and the other to silently keep the old (buggy) behavior.
confirmed.proposedFix: Factor the shared 'walk sm["beats"], accumulate offset, yield each shot with its resolved scene_in/scene_out' logic into one private generator/helper that both scene_retake_rows and scene_shot_windows consume, each just mapping the yielded tuple to its own output dict shape.

Verified directly against engine/cb_address.py (current working tree, lines 139-173).

scene_retake_rows (139-159) and scene_shot_windows (161-173) are indeed near-identical:
- Both call `sm = scene_address_map(pkg_path, scene_num, episode)` and init an accumulator list + `offset = 0.0`.
- Both run the identical nested walk: `for bm in sm["beats"]: for sh in bm.get("shots", []): if "start_sec" not in sh: continue` ... append a dict ... then `offset += bm.get("duration") or 0.0` after the inner loop, at the same indentation/structure.
- They differ ONLY in the shape of the dict appended: scene_retake_rows builds the 13-column CSV row (Scene/Beat/Shot/Ref/Scene In/Scene Out/Beat In/Beat Out/Frames/Current action/blank ISSUE-CHANGE-Priority columns), scene_shot_windows builds the lean {ref, beat, shot, scene_in, scene_out} dict for the burned-in overlay. Even the "scene_in"/"scene_out" value computation (`offset + sh["start_sec"]`, `offset + sh["end_sec"]`) is copy-pasted, just wrapped in `_tc()` in one and `round(..., 3)` in the other.

This is genuine, concrete, verifiable-by-inspection duplication — not a false alarm. It isn't documented anywhere as intentional (no comment near either function acknowledges the twin), and it isn't a case of "looks similar but is actually simple/trivial enough that no one would refactor it" — the shared logic (the offset-accumulation across beats, and the `"start_sec" not in sh` guard that filters out shots from beats whose prompt failed to resolve /unrendered beats) is exactly the kind of behavioral rule that could drift if only one copy gets patched, which is a realistic scenario given this file's own history of "confirmed bug" fixes noted in comments elsewhere in the same file (e.g. the frame-clamp fix, the double-call fix in shot_at_time). The proposed fix (a shared generator yielding resolved shot tuples, consumed by both functions with different output mapping) is sound and proportionate — it wouldn't touch beat_address_map or scene_address_map, just deduplicate these two ~10-line loop bodies.

Severity is correctly self-assessed as low (this is a small, self-contained ~15-line duplication in a single file, easy to keep in sync manually, not a load-bearing correctness risk today) — but "real, low-severity duplication with a plausible future-drift failure mode" is exactly what the finding claims, no more and no less. confirmed.summary: beat_address_map already loads the package JSON and locates the target beat by beatCode/shotCode, then calls cb_seedance.get_seedance_prompt, which reloads the same package file from disk and re-runs the identical 'find beat by code' lookup two more times internally (once in build_for_beat, again in get_seedance_prompt's own definitive-prompt block) — the same one-line lookup idiom this codebase repeats in 28 places across 16 files with no shared helper.
confirmed.failure_scenario: scene_address_map calls beat_address_map once per beat in a scene, so addressing a 5-beat scene parses and re-scans the same package JSON up to 15 times for what is logically one lookup per beat — wasted I/O that scales with scene/episode size, and (in principle) a window where the file could change between reads within a single beat_address_map call, silently breaking the 'same beat object' assumption the function relies on.
confirmed.proposedFix: Have beat_address_map pass its already-loaded beat data into the prompt-building call instead of a bare path (a build_for_beat_from_data-style entry point), or at minimum factor 'load package + find beat by code' into one shared helper reused across cb_address.py and cb_seedance.py rather than each module re-implementing the same lookup.

Verified directly against the current code (engine/cb_address.py and engine/cb_seedance.py).

beat_address_map (cb_address.py:60-65) loads the package JSON and does a linear scan to find the beat by beatCode/shotCode. It then calls cb_seedance.get_seedance_prompt (line 88), which:
1. calls build_for_beat (cb_seedance.py:1320-1323), which independently does `json.load(open(pkg_path))` and re-runs the identical `next((b for b in ... if (b.get("beatCode") or b.get("shotCode")) == beat_code), None)` lookup, then
2. inside get_seedance_prompt's own "DEFINITIVE" block (cb_seedance.py:1428-1431) does yet another `json.load(open(pkg_path))` and the same beat lookup again (this time also resolving the scene object), to build the v5 segprompt.

So a single beat_address_map call really does parse the same package file and re-run the same "find beat by code" scan three times (once in cb_address.py itself, twice inside cb_seedance.py), exactly as described. scene_address_map (line 133) then calls beat_address_map once per beat in the scene with a list comprehension, so a 5-beat scene really does trigger on the order of 15 loads/scans for logically one lookup per beat — the arithmetic in the failure scenario checks out. No caching/memoization exists anywhere in either module to mitigate this (grepped for lru_cache/@cache/memo — none found), so every call really does re-parse from disk.

The "repeated one-line lookup idiom" claim is also roughly right: grepping for the beatCode/shotCode find-by-code pattern turns up ~25-26 hits across the engine, in the ballpark of the cited "28 places."

This is genuinely low severity, not urgent — measured a real load of the current 551KB/43-beat production package.json at ~1.7ms per parse, so even ~15 redundant loads costs only tens of milliseconds, and every caller of this chain (write_retake_csv, scene_shot_windows for review-overlay burn-in, cb_retake's splice helpers) fires at most once or twice per scene during a Gate-4/5 post pass or a manual retake — never in a hot per-frame or per-request loop. The "file could change mid-call" race-condition part of the failure scenario is speculative and overstated for this single-user, sequential-edit pipeline. But the core claim — real, verified, unnecessary duplicate file loads and repeated identical lookups scoped exactly as described, with a reasonable low-risk proposed fix (share the loaded beat/package data instead of re-deriving it) — is accurate. This project's own history (e.g. the adjacent shot_at_time fix in this very file, cb_address.py:175-184, which eliminated an identical double-call of scene_shot_windows) shows this exact class of redundant-recompute finding is treated as a legitimate, worth-fixing cleanup here, not dismissed as noise. So this is a real, if minor, duplication finding correctly labeled low severity — not a false alarm.

confirmed.summary: The JOIN CHECK block in run() leaks its extracted temp PNG whenever anything after its creation raises.
confirmed.failure_scenario: For a relay beat, run() creates a temp file via tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix='.png', delete=False), runs ffmpeg to extract the first frame into it, then calls cb_qa.check_join(...) — a real vision-API call — and only calls os.remove(_first) on the success path. If ffmpeg fails to produce a valid frame, or check_join raises (a network timeout/rate-limit on the vision call is exactly the same transient-failure mode CLAUDE.md rule 61 documents happening to the voice-synthesis step), or the subsequent json.dump raises, the whole block's outer `except Exception as je` catches it, prints 'join check skipped', and moves on — but _first is never deleted. Over a long production run with many relay beats this silently accumulates orphaned temp PNGs in the system temp dir. The file's own stitch() function already fixed the identical class of bug with a try/finally (its docstring explicitly calls out 'cleaned up in a finally so a failed ffmpeg run never leaks the scratch file') — that same discipline wasn't applied here.
confirmed.proposedFix: Wrap the frame-extraction + check_join + os.remove sequence in try/finally (or a context manager) so _first is always removed regardless of how the block exits, mirroring stitch()'s own tempfile.mkstemp/finally pattern in this same file.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Read engine/cb_beats.py lines 470-524 directly. The finding is accurate: at line 497, tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix='.png', delete=False) creates _first; ffmpeg (line 499-500, no check=True so it won't raise even on failure) writes to it; cb_qa.check_join (line 502, a real vision-API call) is invoked on it; os.remove(_first) only happens at line 506, after check_join succeeds and before json.dump. The entire sequence (lines 496-511) is wrapped in a single try whose except at line 512 catches ANY exception (ffmpeg producing an unreadable/empty frame causing check_join to raise, a network/rate-limit error on the vision call — the same transient failure class CLAUDE.md rule 61 documents for the voice-synthesis step — or a json.dump serialization failure) and just prints 'join check skipped', never reaching os.remove. This does leak the temp PNG on any such failure.

I also confirmed the proposed fix's premise: the same file's stitch() function (lines 898-918) already uses tempfile.mkstemp + try/finally for its own scratch file, and its docstring explicitly says 'cleaned up in a finally so a failed ffmpeg run never leaks the scratch file' while citing 'the JOIN CHECK's NamedTemporaryFile use above' as the established precedent — confirming the codebase itself considers this the correct pattern, which was applied to stitch() but not back-applied to the JOIN CHECK block it names as prior art. Grepped the file and cb_qa.py for any other cleanup mechanism that might catch this file (e.g., a temp-dir GC) — none exists. confirmed.summary: check_ensemble_individuation resolves a possessive character name (e.g. "Keen's Mum") to the WRONG side of the apostrophe when locating its mention in the beat's action text, causing it to share the other character's own text window — this already-known bug class was fixed in cb_segprompt._v5_active_cast but never swept into this sibling file.

Because both "Keen" and "Keen's Mum" then search for the identical substring "keen" via lower.find(), they resolve to the SAME text window (whichever "keen" occurs first in the whole beat). Confirmed live against the real production package (cb-output/Ep1_The_Adventure_Begins_beat_package.json): beat 3.B7's action text only ever attributes "laughs" to Keen's Mum (cut 1: "Keen's Mum laughs through a tear...") and never to Keen (his own actions are "startles"/"leans over"/"holds the rail"), yet check_ensemble_individuation emits the flag "Keen, Keen's Mum are each given the near-identical action verb 'laugh'" — factually wrong, both names collapsed onto the same window. 2. The logging claim is also accurate: `_norm_line` (line 342-346) strips a leading `NAME:` prefix before comparing. If only the speaker label differs (identical wording), `_norm_line(cut.get("dialogue")) == _norm_line(line)` is true, so the per-line "verbatim ... corrected" log (line 368) is skipped even though `cut["dialogue"] = want` still executes and `fixed` still increments — confirmed by reading the exact branch structure. The proposed fix (mirror `_force_include`'s characters/speakers/openingCast bookkeeping, and log on any dialogue-string change rather than only word-level changes) is correct, feasible, and consistent with the codebase's own established pattern.

confirmed.summary: CB_DIRECTOR_PASS/CB_DIRECTOR_PASS_REFRESH boolean env-var parsing is case-sensitive except for two hardcoded castings, unlike the .strip().lower() idiom this codebase already uses for the same purpose elsewhere.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Line 135: os.environ.get('CB_DIRECTOR_PASS', '1') in ('', '0', 'false', 'False', 'no') -- setting CB_DIRECTOR_PASS=OFF or =FALSE (all caps) matches none of these literals, so the Director's Pass silently stays ON when a user believes they disabled it. cb_llm.py:35 and cb_retake.py:216 both solve the identical problem with .strip().lower() in (...).
confirmed.proposedFix: Normalize with .strip().lower() before the membership check, matching cb_llm.py/cb_retake.py's existing convention.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified directly against the cited file. engine/cb_director_pass.py:135 reads `os.environ.get(\"CB_DIRECTOR_PASS\", \"1\") in (\"\", \"0\", \"false\", \"False\", \"no\")` and line 140 has the identical pattern for CB_DIRECTOR_PASS_REFRESH — neither normalizes case/whitespace before the membership check, only hardcoding two case variants of the word \"false\" (lowercase and capitalized). No comment or design rationale in cb_director_pass.py justifies the different, case-sensitive treatment — it reads as an oversight, not a documented exception. ph = str(b.get("pauseHold") or "")

confirmed.summary: _generate_image_seedream — the function generate_image() now dispatches to by default (IMAGE_PROVIDER='seedream', rule 60, 2026-07-09) — never sends the requested aspect ratio or resolution to the Seedream API; both are silently dropped.
confirmed.failure_scenario: generate_image(prompt, refs, aspect='16:9', out, model=None, image_size='2K') dispatches to _generate_image_seedream(prompt, refs, aspect, out) when no model= override is given. Inside that function the fal args dict built at line 142 is `{'prompt': prompt, 'image_urls': ref_urls}` only — no aspect_ratio/image_size key anywhere — and the function's signature doesn't even accept an image_size parameter, so generate_image()'s own image_size='2K' default never reaches this path at all (compare _generate_image_nanobanana, lines 160-178, which correctly builds imageConfig={'aspectRatio':aspect,'imageSize':image_size}). Every one of cb_scene.py's ~14 call sites passes aspect='16:9' expecting a 16:9 keyframe at 2K; under the current default provider that request is never actually made to the model, so the rendered keyframe's aspect/resolution is whatever Seedream infers or defaults to, with no error, warning, or QA check catching a mismatch. The write_gen_sidecar call at line 156-157 even logs aspect=aspect into the reproducibility sidecar, so the sidecar will claim 16:9 was requested even when it wasn't — the exact 'why does this differ from what shipped' gap rule 57's own sidecar was built to close.
confirmed.proposedFix: Add the aspect ratio (and, if the fal endpoint supports it, an explicit size/resolution field) into the args dict passed to _fal_subscribe(SEEDREAM_ENDPOINT, ...), mirroring the imageConfig pattern already used in _generate_image_nanobanana; add an image_size parameter to _generate_image_seedream and forward it from generate_image()'s dispatcher so the existing image_size argument actually reaches the new default provider.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified directly against engine/cb_gen.py (lines 119-158) and its real callers.

`generate_image()` (line 120) dispatches to `_generate_image_seedream(prompt, refs, aspect, out)` (line 130) for every default call — i.e. every one of `cb_scene.py`'s ~14 call sites, all confirmed via grep to pass `aspect="16:9"` positionally and rely on `generate_image`'s `image_size="2K"` default, and none pass `model=`.

`_generate_image_seedream`'s signature (line 132) is `(prompt, refs=None, aspect="16:9", out="keyframe.png")` — no `image_size` parameter at all. Its body builds `args = {"prompt": prompt, "image_urls": ref_urls}` (line 142) — literally no aspect/size key of any kind — before calling `_fal_subscribe(SEEDREAM_ENDPOINT, arguments=args, ...)`. The `aspect` parameter is used for exactly one thing in the whole function: logged into `write_gen_sidecar(..., aspect=aspect, ...)` at line 156, so the reproducibility sidecar claims a 16:9 request was made even though it wasn't. This is a real, verifiable dead-parameter bug, not a stylistic nitpick.

By contrast `_generate_image_nanobanana` (lines 160-178) correctly threads both through as `img_cfg = {"aspectRatio": aspect, "imageSize": image_size}` inside `generationConfig` — confirming the Seedream path is missing parity with its sibling, not that aspect/size are unnecessary for this class of call.

Checked the claimed mitigating/refuting angles and found they don't hold:
- `test_cb_gen.py`'s 12 passing tests only monkeypatch `_generate_image_seedream` itself out entirely — they test routing logic, never the args dict this function actually builds, so "12/12 passing" gives zero real coverage of this bug.
- `cb_qa.check_done_frame` does have a deterministic `BAD_ASPECT`/`LOW_RESOLUTION` check (`DONE_MIN_WIDTH=2048`, aspect window 1.70-1.85) wired into `check_scene`, itself called from `cb_pipeline.py` at Gate 2 sign-off points — so a wrong-aspect/low-res keyframe would eventually be caught by QA rather than silently shipping to Gate 3. This softens (but does not refute) the finding: it means the practical failure mode is wasted generation spend + rework loops, not necessarily an undetected bad frame reaching render — but the finding's core claim ("aspect/resolution are silently dropped from the actual API call") is accurate and the "no error/warning catches it at generation time" framing is basically right (nothing at generation time itself warns; the catch, if any, comes later at a QA gate). Real reference turnaround images sampled (1376×768, well under the 2048 floor) show the risk is not merely theoretical — if Seedream infers size from references rather than defaulting to something reasonable, it's plausible to get 2K-floor failures routinely.

This is a real, concrete, high-severity correctness bug: a parameter the caller explicitly requests (16:9, 2K) is silently never transmitted to the model that is now the production default, contradicting the function's own docstring claim of contract parity with the NB2 path it replaced.

confirmed.summary: _generate_image_nanobanana hand-rolls its own 429/500/503 retry-with-backoff loop instead of reusing this same file's own _retry()/_rpost() utility a few lines above it — and a third, again-different retry policy for the identical failure class already exists in cb_qa.py's vision_verdict().
confirmed.failure_scenario: Lines 70-109 define one shared, jitter-backed retry abstraction (_retry/_retryable, used consistently by _rpost/_rget/_fal_upload/_fal_subscribe: 4 tries, exponential backoff+jitter capped at 60s, with real 4xx-vs-5xx/429 classification). _generate_image_nanobanana (lines 180-198) ignores it entirely: it calls raw requests.post via a local _post() closure and manually loops `for attempt in range(5)` checking resp.status_code directly (no raise_for_status, no jitter, its own 8/16/32/60/60s schedule). cb_qa.vision_verdict (cb_qa.py ~lines 78-97) independently reimplements yet a third version for the same Gemini-API transient-failure class (3 tries, 4*2**attempt capped at 20s, no jitter). Three divergent policies for one failure mode mean a future tuning change (raising try-count, adding a retryable status) has to be hunted down and applied in three places, and they've already drifted from each other in tries/backoff/jitter.
confirmed.proposedFix: Route _generate_image_nanobanana's request through _rpost (keeping only the bespoke 'retry aspect-only on a 400 imageSize rejection' branch as special-case logic before the shared retry takes over), and consider having cb_qa.vision_verdict call cb_gen._rpost as well, since it already imports cb_gen for _b64/GLA/GEMINI_KEY.
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified directly against the current code in engine/cb_gen.py and engine/cb_qa.py — every factual claim in the finding checks out exactly:

1. Shared abstraction (cb_gen.py lines 70-109): `_retry()` (tries=4, base=4.0, cap=60.0, `wait = min(cap, base*(2**(attempt-1))) + random.uniform(0,1.0)` — exponential backoff with jitter) plus `_retryable()`'s real 4xx-vs-5xx/429 classification, consistently used by `_rpost`/`_rget`/`_fal_upload`/`_fal_subscribe`.

2. `_generate_image_nanobanana` (lines 160-212, the cited loop at line 192): defines its own local `_post()` closure calling raw `requests.post` (line 180-183), checks `resp.status_code` directly with no `raise_for_status`/no exception path, and hand-loops `for attempt in range(5): ... wait = min(60, 8*(2**attempt))` (line 192-198) — a second, textually different backoff schedule (8/16/32/60/60s, no jitter) for the identical 429/500/503 failure class the shared `_retry` already exists to handle.

3. `cb_qa.vision_verdict` (confirmed via grep, lines 78-98): imports `cb_gen` already (line 21 of cb_qa.py: `import cb_gen, cb_prompts as P`), yet reimplements a THIRD retry loop from scratch — `for attempt in range(3): ... time.sleep(min(20, 4*(2**attempt)))` — for the same Gemini-API transient-error class, with no jitter and a different cap/try-count than either of the other two.

All three loops target the identical failure mode (429/500/503/transient network fault on a Gemini/fal-style JSON HTTP call) with three genuinely divergent, hand-rolled schedules. This is not a cosmetic style complaint: `_retry()` already accepts `tries`/`base`/`cap` as parameters, so both the nanobanana loop and `vision_verdict` could delegate to it (customizing budget where a shorter QA-check timeout is genuinely wanted) instead of re-deriving the backoff math independently — meaning there's no real technical barrier that forced this duplication, only that it wasn't done. It's exactly the kind of "same pattern re-implemented instead of swept/unified" issue this codebase's own CLAUDE.md explicitly treats as a standing defect class (rule 11's "hunt the same pattern across every module," rule 56's contradiction/duplication sweep), and it is a real, live risk today: this file's own historical comments show the shared retry policy has already been tuned once (the "TICKET 5" resilience pass) — a future tuning of try-count/backoff/retryable-status-set has to be found and applied in three places by hand, and they've already drifted from each other.

The only plausible refutation — that `_generate_image_nanobanana`'s special 400-imageSize-rejection handling requires inspecting a raw response before `_rpost`'s `raise_for_status`-based flow could apply — only justifies why the *400-specific* branch is bespoke, not why the *separate* 429/500/503 loop (the actual cited code, lines 190-198) needed to be reimplemented from scratch rather than delegating to `_retry`/`_retryable` once the request body was finalized. The proposed fix's own phrasing ("keeping only the bespoke... branch as special-case logic before the shared retry takes over") already accounts for this and is a workable refactor. Severity "medium" for a "duplication" category is appropriately calibrated — this is real tech debt, not a functional bug, and matches how this project's own prior audit (rule 59) treated comparable duplicated-helper findings.

confirmed.summary: lipsync() indexes result['video']['url'] directly with no defensive check, unlike every sibling video-generation function in the same file, which all guard against a missing/error-shaped fal response.
confirmed.failure_scenario: generate_video_seedance, generate_video_seedance_ref, and _generate_image_seedream all do `url = (result.get('video') or {}).get('url')` (or the images/image equivalent) then `if not url: raise SystemExit(f'... returned no video url: {result}')`, so a failed/malformed fal response fails loud with the actual response body for debugging. lipsync() (line 403) instead does `url = result['video']['url']` directly — if fal ever returns an error shape (e.g. `{'error': ...}`, no 'video' key — the exact failure mode the sibling functions were written to handle), this raises a bare KeyError with no diagnostic content instead of a clear SystemExit naming what actually came back.
confirmed.proposedFix: Apply the same `(result.get('video') or {}).get('url')` + explicit `SystemExit` naming the raw response pattern already used by generate_video_seedance/generate_video_seedance_ref.
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified directly against engine/cb_gen.py. Line 403's `lipsync()` does `url = result[\"video\"][\"url\"]` with no defensive check. Its three siblings in the same file all guard: generate_video_seedance (lines 324-326: `url = (result.get('video') or {}).get('url'); if not url: raise SystemExit(f\"Seedance returned no video url: {result}\")`), generate_video_seedance_ref (lines 379-381, identical pattern), and _generate_image_seedream (lines 144-150, same pattern for the image-key variants). The finding's summary and failure scenario are factually accurate — a fal error-shaped response (e.g. `{'error': ...}`, no 'video' key) would raise a bare, undiagnostic KeyError in lipsync() while every sibling function would instead raise a SystemExit naming the actual response body. This is a genuine, easily-reproduced inconsistency, not a false alarm — the 'duplication' the sibling functions show is clearly an intentional, repeated defensive pattern that this one function simply never received. ONE REAL FLAW IN THE FINDING'S SCOPE, WORTH NOTING: `cb_director_schemas.py`/`cb_director.py` explicitly document that `characters` deliberately includes cast members who "enter LATER in the beat" and are NOT in `openingCast` (line 605-606: "A character who ENTERS LATER in the beat is listed in 'characters' but NOT here"). Zenny held frame-right"). For the END-frame check (`is_end=True`, used on the clip's "last" extracted frame) and for `_passB` (which spans keyframe+first+mid+last as ONE continuity window), using the fuller `characters` list is arguably the semantically correct behavior, not a bug — a blanket swap to `P.opening_cast(shot)` in both functions, as the proposed fix literally states, would introduce a NEW regression: legitimately late-arriving cast members (Zenny in 6.B2, similar ensemble beats) would start false-flagging as EXTRA_CHARACTER/CLIP_POP_CHARACTER on correctly-rendered final frames.

confirmed.summary: The idle-reload guard in _freshness_watch() only checks PROCS (tracked async render jobs), not any other in-flight HTTP request thread, before calling os.execv() to reload the process.
confirmed.failure_scenario: serve.py is edited while the studio is running and no async render job is active (PROCS empty). Several handlers do real, non-trivial work synchronously in a request thread and are never registered in PROCS: approve_gate/unapprove_gate/set_master_studio/clear_master_studio (each a blocking subprocess.run against cb_pipeline.py), plus the read-only preview endpoints (/api/masters, /api/keyframe-prompt, /api/voice-prompt, /api/beat-sound-brief, /api/beat-prompt, /api/retake-brief, /api/export-storyboard), and _serve_static's own chunked video/range streaming loop. If the 3-second freshness poll fires while any of these is mid-flight, os.execv() replaces the whole process image: per POSIX, every thread but the calling one is terminated immediately, and Python's sockets are close-on-exec by default, so that thread's client connection is dropped outright (a failed fetch in the browser, or a video stream cut off mid-seek) even though a spawned child subprocess for that request (e.g. the cb_pipeline.py approve call) may go on to finish and write locked.json on its own, unseen by the client that asked for it.
confirmed.proposedFix: Track in-flight requests with a simple counter/lock (increment at the top of do_GET/do_POST, decrement in a finally), and have _freshness_watch()/_is_stale()-triggered reload check that counter alongside `not PROCS` before calling _reexec() — the same 'only reload when truly idle' intent the PROCS check already expresses for async jobs, extended to synchronous ones.

I read the actual code and could not refute this — it holds up as a real, concrete gap.

Confirmed facts from the file:
1. `_freshness_watch()` (lines 33-42) polls every 3s and calls `_reexec()` (which does `os.execv()`, line 32) whenever `_is_stale() and not PROCS` — PROCS is the ONLY guard (line 148: "PROCS = {} # jobId -> Popen", populated only by the async `/api/fire` render-job path at lines 299-310/336).
2. Several handlers do real, non-trivial, purely synchronous work in the request thread and are never added to PROCS: `approve_gate`/`unapprove_gate`/`set_master_studio`/`clear_master_studio` (lines 397-424) each call blocking `subprocess.run(...)` directly (not `Popen` + PROCS-tracked) — `set_master_studio` even has a 150s timeout, meaning this is expected to legitimately take a long time. These are called synchronously from `do_POST` (lines 1014, 1022, 1039, 1048).
3. The read-only preview endpoints (`/api/masters`, `/api/keyframe-prompt`, `/api/voice-prompt`, `/api/beat-sound-brief`, `/api/beat-prompt`, `/api/retake-brief`, `/api/export-storyboard` — lines 685, 810, 826, 846, 877, 961, 1003) likewise run blocking `subprocess.run` calls in-thread, untracked.
4. `_serve_static` (lines 587-661) streams video/audio in a real chunked loop (256KB reads, line 651-659) for potentially large files with Range/seek support — this can run for a nontrivial duration in its own thread.
5. The server is `http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer` (line 1435, confirmed `ThreadingMixIn` behavior — one thread per connection), so all of the above genuinely run concurrently with the freshness-watch thread, not serially.
6. No in-flight-request counter, lock, or any other tracking mechanism exists anywhere in the file (grepped for `Lock()`, `in_flight`, `active_requests`, `request_count` — zero hits). `/api/restart` (line 922-924) has the identical gap (`if PROCS:` only), reinforcing that PROCS was never meant to cover synchronous work.

On the technical mechanism itself: Python sockets are non-inheritable (close-on-exec) by default since PEP 446 (Python 3.4+), for both the listening socket and accepted client sockets, and POSIX `exec()` semantics do terminate every thread but the calling one instantly, without running their cleanup — so a genuinely in-flight synchronous handler or a mid-stream video chunk write in another thread is exactly as exposed as the finding describes.

I found no comment, doctrine note, or memory entry (including the "Studio freshness guard" memory bullet) that acknowledges or accepts this specific "idle" is scoped to PROCS only rather than all in-flight work — it isn't a documented, intentional trade-off. The proposed fix (a simple in-flight counter checked alongside `not PROCS`) is a reasonable, proportionate remedy. Severity "medium" is fair for a locally-run dev tool where the failure window only opens while actively editing serve.py during a live session.

confirmed.summary: record_chain_source() sorts a scene's beats with a plain lexicographic str() key instead of the shared cb_preflight._beat_sort_key, so for any scene with 10+ beats it will resolve the wrong predecessor beat when stamping the FRAME CHAIN cascade's baseline hash.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Once any scene grows to 10+ beats (current max in the live Ep1 package is 8, Scene 3 — so this is latent, not yet firing), beats.sort(key=lambda b: str(b.get('beatCode') or b.get('shotCode') or '')) places e.g. '5.B10' between '5.B1' and '5.B2' (lexicographic '1' < '10' < '2'). record_chain_source computes i = index of the target beat in that mis-sorted list and sets prev = beats[i-1], then stamps prev's harvested-ending-frame hash as chain_source_fp. For every beat whose natural-order predecessor doesn't match its lexicographic-order predecessor, this silently stamps the WRONG beat's ending-frame hash as the chain baseline — corrupting the drift-detection baseline CLAUDE.md rule 15/21's FRAME CHAIN cascade depends on, with no error or warning raised.
confirmed.proposedFix: Replace `beats.sort(key=lambda b: str(b.get('beatCode') or b.get('shotCode') or ''))` with `beats.sort(key=lambda b: cb_preflight._beat_sort_key(b.get('beatCode') or b.get('shotCode') or ''))`. cb_preflight is already imported lazily 3x elsewhere in this same file (lines 245/308/759) and cb_preflight.py does not import cb_pipeline, so a module-level `import cb_preflight` is safe. This matches the fix already applied to this file's own export_storyboard() (line 246) and to cb_beats.fire_next_beat / cb_previz._beats_for_scene / cb_replicator.walk_scene / cb_director._derive_performance_throughline — all cited by name in export_storyboard's own comment, which never mentions this sibling function 190 lines earlier in the same file.

A retaken upstream beat's new ending frame could fail to dirty the correct downstream beats (a stale keyframe/clip lock silently left valid), or could wrongly dirty an unrelated beat — defeating the auto-relock guarantee CLAUDE.md rule 15/21 promises, with no error surfaced. Because this function and record_chain_source independently re-derive 'the previous beat' from the same broken sort, both must be fixed together or they can disagree with each other even after one is patched.

Add a regression test alongside test_gate_cascade.py's existing scene-9 case (which only exercises 2-3 beats, e.g. '9.B1'..'9.B3', and would not catch this) — a scratch scene with an 11th beat ('N.B10') verifying the resolved predecessor is beat 9, not beat 1.
confirmed.sourceLabel: grep the whole engine/ tree for beat-code natural-sort logic
confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Confirmed real. Read engine/cb_pipeline.py directly: record_chain_source (line 109) and _relock_chain_if_dirty (line 140) both sort a scene's beats with `beats.sort(key=lambda b: str(b.get(\"beatCode\") or b.get(\"shotCode\") or \"\"))` — a plain lexicographic string sort — then use positional adjacency (`beats[i-1]` / `scene_beats[i-1]`) to identify each beat's chain predecessor. I traced this by hand for an 11-beat scene: lexicographic order puts \"1.B10\" immediately after \"1.B1\" and before \"1.B2\" (since '1.B1' is a string-prefix of '1.B10', and '1.B10' < '1.B2' because '1' < '2' at the first differing character). This misassigns the predecessor for beat B2 (gets B11 instead of B1) and B10 (gets B1 instead of B9) — exactly the failure scenario described.

This is the identical bug class CLAUDE.md rule 59 documents finding and fixing in four other places (cb_beats.fire_next_beat, cb_director._derive_performance_throughline, cb_previz._beats_for_scene, cb_replicator.walk_scene), all swept to use the shared cb_preflight._beat_sort_key natural-sort helper (confirmed via grep — it exists and is used at 5+ other call sites, including elsewhere in this same file at line 246). The sweep evidently missed these two functions in cb_pipeline.py.

Checked for a false-alarm explanation: line 57's identical-looking plain sort (_scene_beats_fingerprint) is NOT the same bug — it only needs a deterministic order to hash consistently, not a story-correct order, so that one is fine and distinct from the flagged lines. No CLAUDE.md rule or code comment reconciles or exempts record_chain_source/_relock_chain_if_dirty from the natural-sort fix. The existing test (test_frame_chain_cascade in test_gate_cascade.py) only covers a 3-beat scene (9.B1-9.B3), which cannot expose the bug since single-digit suffixes sort correctly — confirming the proposed test gap is real. Currently latent in production (max scene size is 8 beats, scene 3) but a genuine, reproducible correctness bug the moment any scene reaches 10 beats, silently breaking the auto-relock cascade CLAUDE.md rules 15/21 promise. The proposed fix (apply cb_preflight._beat_sort_key, same as line 109's neighbor at line 246) is correct and consistent with the established fix pattern.

confirmed.verifierReasoning:
I read the cited code directly and the finding holds up.

Confirmed facts:
1. `_relock_if_stale()` (cb_pipeline.py lines 61-86) pops GATE_SEQ entries + "2"/"1_fp" from locked.json and clears `sd["beats"]` — it never touches `config/locations.json`.
2. `unapprove(gate, scene)` (lines 368-415) explicitly resets `locations.json`'s scene `master` field to `None` whenever `gate in ("1", "2a")` (line 409-415) — a real, deliberate side effect the manual path performs that the automatic path does not.
3. Grep confirms `locations.json`'s `master` key is written in exactly two places in the whole engine: `_lock_plate_as_master` (line 216, called only from `approve("2a", ...)`) and `unapprove`'s reset (line 414). `_relock_if_stale` is not one of them — matching the finding's grep claim exactly.
4. `build_beat()` (line 769) never calls `_approved()`/`_relock_if_stale` anywhere — it only calls `_manifest_gate_beat()`, which routes through `cb_preflight.manifest_ok()` (confirmed via imports — cb_preflight.py never imports cb_pipeline or touches locked.json). That check is a content/manifest-completeness check (endState, humourLayer, etc.) and explicitly never checks plate/gate-lock status ("The plate is NEVER a manifest BLOCK, in any gate scope"). So it provides zero protection against a stale sign-off.
5. `cb_scene.build_one_beat`'s only gate is `has_plate = bool(master and os.path.exists(master))` read via `P.scene_cfg` → `locations.json`'s `master` field directly — existence-only, no recency/approval check.
6. By contrast, `coverage()`/`rebuild()` (the whole-scene Gate-2b path) DO call `_approved(scene, "2a")` before reaching `cb_scene.run()`, so they correctly refuse once auto-relock clears "2a" in locked.json — exactly the asymmetry the finding describes.

This is not merely a hypothetical severity call — `_relock_if_stale`'s own docstring states it cascade-clears "exactly like unapprove('1', scene)," but it demonstrably does not: `unapprove` resets the master on a "1"/"2a" clear and this function doesn't, so the code fails to deliver on its own stated equivalence contract.

Mitigating factor I checked for and found real but incomplete: `cb-studio/serve.py`'s `/api/gen-keyframe` endpoint (the actual Studio-UI front door that spawns the `build-beat` subprocess) does check `_scene_locks(scene, episode).get("2a")` first, and serve.py's own mirrored `_relock_stale_scenes` correctly clears "2a" from locked.json — so the described failure scenario is blocked when fired through the normal Studio UI. However: (a) `cb_pipeline.py build-beat` is directly CLI-invocable with zero self-defense — the only two call sites for `build_beat()` are its definition and the bare `__main__` dispatch, so nothing stops a direct CLI call (or any future non-Studio caller — a script, a test, a new automation) from firing a real generation off a stale master; (b) this is precisely the same bug class (a per-beat function lacking a check its whole-scene sibling has) that rule 46 in this project's own history already found and fixed once for the manifest check — the gate-lock/master-staleness version of that exact gap was simply never closed. Given the codebase's own stated doctrine on sweep-the-pattern and defense-in-depth, and that the underlying facts are all directly verified in the code (not inferred), I judge this a real, concrete finding, not a false alarm — medium severity is a fair rating given the serve.py mitigation narrows (but does not eliminate) the practical blast radius.

confirmed.summary: approve()/unapprove() never validate that the `gate` argument is an actual member of GATE_SEQ before proceeding. _prev_gate() (line 178-180) silently returns None for an unrecognized gate string, which approve() treats identically to gate='1' (no predecessor to check) — so `python3 cb_pipeline.py approve foo 1` writes an unvalidated `sd['foo'] = {...}` sign-off into locked.json. fire() is stricter (`if gate not in GATES: return False`, line 959-960); approve()/unapprove() have no equivalent guard.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A typo'd or future-renamed gate string (e.g. 'approve 2A 1' with wrong case handled fine by .lower(), but 'approve 2 1' or 'approve foo 1') silently succeeds and pollutes locked.json with a bogus key, with no error surfaced. Currently harmless in practice since nothing else in the chain reads an arbitrary key as a real predecessor (_prev_gate only ever resolves real GATE_SEQ members), but it's a silent acceptance of invalid input where the sibling function (fire) is correctly strict.
confirmed.proposedFix: Add `if gate not in GATE_SEQ: print(...); return False` to the top of approve() and unapprove(), matching fire()'s existing `gate not in GATES` guard.

Neither approve() nor unapprove() has a `gate not in GATE_SEQ` guard anywhere in their bodies (read in full), unlike fire() (lines 958-960) which explicitly checks `if gate not in GATES: print(...); return False`.

confirmed.verifierReasoning:
Verified directly against the code, and the finding holds up.

1. `cb-studio/serve.py:205` (`def locked_state()`) calls only `_relock_stale_scenes(d)` (line 212), whose own docstring says it "cascade-clears any scene whose Gate-1 fingerprint has drifted" — it compares `sd["1_fp"]` against `_scene_beats_fingerprint`. It never touches `_relock_chain_if_dirty`'s territory: `grep -c "chain_source_fp\|_relock_chain\|harvest_settle_frame" cb-studio/serve.py` returns 0.

2. `engine/cb_pipeline.py` has a genuinely separate, second staleness mechanism — `_relock_chain_if_dirty` (lines 125-170), which hashes each beat's harvested settle frame (`_beat_end_frame_hash`) and cascade-clears downstream `keyframe`/`clip` per-beat locks when an upstream beat's settle frame changes (a retake). `_approved()` (line 172-176) calls *both* `_relock_if_stale(scene)` and `_relock_chain_if_dirty(scene)`, and `_approved` is in fact called from `approve()` (347), `regen()` (437, 456, 477), `coverage()` (607), `rebuild()` (633, 649), `set_master()` (688), and `fire()` (962) — matching the finding's claim exactly.

3. Tracing the actual retake flow (`regen()` with `kind="clip"`) confirms the gap is live, not just theoretical: its own `_approved(scene, "2b")` gate-check fires *before* `cb_beats.run(...)` performs the render and writes the new settle frame, so this same call can't observe the staleness the retake is about to create. No subsequent call to `_relock_chain_if_dirty` happens inside `regen()` after the render. `cb_beats.py`/`cb_scene.py`/`cb_replicator.py` were grepped clean of any `chain_source`/`_relock` calls — nothing else re-triggers the chain check either. So the downstream beat's `keyframe`/`clip` per-beat locks in `locked.json` stay `True` until some *other*, unrelated gate action for that scene happens to call `_approved()` again.

4. Strong in-repo corroboration of the exact same bug class: `cb_replicator.py`'s `_gate2b_signed` docstring (dated 2026-07-08, labelled "confirmed HIGH bug") explicitly distinguishes the two mechanisms — "`cb_pipeline._approved` calls `_relock_if_stale` + `_relock_chain_if_dirty`; serve.py's `locked_state()` calls `_relock_stale_scenes`" (singular) — an existing code comment already documents that serve.py's mirror is narrower than `_approved`, just without itself closing that gap. `test_gate_cascade.py`'s `test_frame_chain_cascade` only exercises `cb_pipeline.py`'s own function directly; `test_serve_py` only exercises the fingerprint mirror — there is no test anywhere covering serve.py against frame-chain dirtiness, so nothing would catch a regression here.

One caveat on severity/impact, worth noting but not disqualifying: the per-beat `keyframe`/`clip` flags are purely a UI/status-display concern (`beatStageLocked` in app.html renders a checkmark from them) — they don't gate what the actual render pipeline does, since `cb_beats.run`/`relay_source_for` reads real settle-frame files directly, not these lock flags. So this doesn't corrupt output; it does produce a misleading "✓ signed off" in the Studio UI, which is exactly the invariant serve.py's own comment claims to guarantee never happens ("the Pipeline page can never show a stale 'signed off' again") — a real, confirmed violation of that stated guarantee for the frame-chain case specifically, distinct from the Gate-1-fingerprint case it does handle.

confirmed.summary: _pkg_name()/reindex_episodes()/_scene_beats_fingerprint() in serve.py pre-sort candidate package files with sorted(...) before taking max-mtime, while cb_pipeline._resolve_pkg() takes max-mtime over an unsorted glob.glob() result — the two tie-breaking algorithms are not textually identical.
confirmed.failure_scenario: If two beat-package files for the same episode ever exist with an identical mtime (e.g. copied together, or a coarse-mtime filesystem), cb_pipeline.py could resolve to a different package file than serve.py displays/hashes, reintroducing the exact 'display != fire' class of bug this project already fixed once (see the 'one Ep1 package' doctrine). Currently masked by the enforced one-package-per-episode convention.
confirmed.proposedFix: Make both resolvers use the identical tie-break rule (e.g. both sort candidates the same way before taking max, or both rely purely on unsorted glob order) so a future duplicate-package edge case can't silently diverge.
confirmed.sourceLabel: Trace the SAME gate sequencing logic in cb-studio/serve.py (
confirmed.verifierReasoning: Verified directly against current code. cb-studio/serve.py's _pkg_name() (line 155-160) and _scene_beats_fingerprint() (line 169-174) both compute `cands = sorted(OUT.glob(...)) or sorted(OUT.glob(...))` then `max(cands, key=lambda p: p.stat().st_mtime)` — pre-sorted by filename before max-by-mtime. engine/cb_pipeline.py's _resolve_pkg() (line 16-21) computes `cands = glob.glob(...) or glob.glob(...)` (unsorted) then `max(cands, key=os.path.getmtime)` — no filename pre-sort. Because Python's max() only advances its running-best on a strictly-greater key, a genuine mtime tie resolves to the first candidate in iteration order — filename-sorted order in serve.py vs. raw/arbitrary os.scandir order in cb_pipeline.py — so the two resolvers can diverge on a tie. This is not already reconciled: serve.py's own docstring calls it a 'mirror' of cb_pipeline._resolve_pkg, and a nearby comment claims 'Same key on both = they can never diverge again,' but that claim only covers sort direction (oldest-first-so-newest-wins in reindex_episodes' dict-merge), not the tie-break order used by max() in these two specific functions — so the comment is itself slightly overclaiming and doesn't actually cover this gap. I also confirmed there is no code-level guard preventing two package files from coexisting for the same episode (the only place stale packages are removed is the episode-delete handler at serve.py:1179), so the 'masked by the enforced one-package-per-episode convention' caveat in the finding is accurate — it's a practice/discipline guarantee, not an enforced invariant. Severity is correctly scored low (masked in the common case, a real gap only on an actual mtime tie), but it is a real, concrete, correctly-described issue, not a false alarm.

Verified directly against the current source. engine/cb_scene.py's relay_source_for (line ~261) and chain_source_for (line ~341) both locate "the previous beat" via `idx = <index of code>`, then `j = idx - 1` (walking back over vision beats only) — raw array-index adjacency with zero natural-sort/reordering of the `beats` list passed in. I also diffed the working tree's own recent, still-uncommitted changes to cb_scene.py (git diff) covering its own "2 findings" fix pass (not-found-vs-first distinction, stale-harvest freshness check, safe char_identity_ref, live HANDLE_SETTLE import) — none of these touched the sort-order gap either, confirming it slipped through both the file-specific pass and the project-wide rule-59 sweep.

The failure scenario is real and correctly scoped as latent, not active: I confirmed cb-studio/serve.py's /api/beat-update (lines 1223-1258) mutates the target beat dict in place within the existing list and never reorders or inserts into the array, and the finding correctly states current production scenes are already in narrative order — so this is a genuine but currently-dormant correctness bug, not a false alarm.
